newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS-PolyGram falls on profit warning.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-PolyGram falls on profit warning.

text.p: PolyGram NV issued a surprise profit warning on Wednesday, triggering a sharp slide in the music and film group's share price.
PolyGram said operating profits for 1996 would be flat or slightly below those of 1995 because compact disc and cassette sales had fallen short of its expectations.

"Entering the important fourth quarter the company currently expects the full-year 1996 operating result before restructuring charges to be flat or slightly below last year's, caused by lower than expected music sales," it said in a statement.
PolyGram said it had fallen victim to sluggish music markets worldwide but added that music sales were also lower than expected due to problems specific to PolyGram.
On the Amsterdam stock exchange PolyGram shares fell 5.60 guilders or 6.6 percent to 79.30 guilders as investors baulked at the prospect of a second straight year of flat earnings.
The company -- 75 percent owned by Dutch giant Philips Electronics NV -- said it would take a $90 million reorganisation charge against its 1996 results and cut 400 jobs.
The shake-up will focus on Motown, the black U.S. pop label acquired in 1993, PolyGram's classical music division and its European marketing and distribution operations.
But analysts said stagnant markets could stalk PolyGram for several years and that even tougher measures might be necessary.
"I do not see the stagnation as temporary, as PolyGram would have us believe," said Rene Verhoef of brokerage NIBStrating.
Verhoef noted that CD sales were no longer being supported by consumers replacing worn-out LPs.
"Margins in the industry are also under pressure as department stores want to purchase music more cheaply," he said, adding that the malaise could continue for several more years.

The profit warning heralds a second year of virtually flat profit growth for PolyGram which saw net profit creep up to 741 million guilders ($431 million) in 1995, almost unchanged from 738 million in 1994.
PolyGram spokeswoman Amanda Conroy said a rejuvenation of Motown was a key goal of the planned restructuring.

"Management is taking positive steps to...make sure that the (Motown) label rejuvenates itself with new artists," she said. "It has a fantastic back catalogue, obviously, but any record label needs to bring on new artists."
Conroy said PolyGram was also taking action to offset the effects of a flat market for classical music recordings.
"The way we're addressing this problem at PolyGram is to revamp our three classical labels -- Decca, Deutsche Grammophon, Philips Classics," she said.

Analyst Joost van Beek of brokers Van Meer James Capel said he expected PolyGram's earnings per share to drop to around 4.00 guilders in 1996 from 4.12 guilders in 1995 but added that they could recover to around 4.50 in 1997, supported in the longer term by the growth of the group's film business.
Van Beek said he saw no reason to change his forecast for Thursday's third quarter earnings from Philips.
Analysts expect Philips' third-quarter net profit from ordinary operations to drop to 240-360 million guilders, far below the equivalent 1995 figure of 539 million guilders.
